Demonstrates that final-response evaluation is insufficient: unsafe behavior emerges in intermediate tool calls/file writes while the user-facing task still completes.
notes: Method = reward-guided beam search + reflection deep probing; benchmark = 42 cases / 6 risk classes / 7 scenarios. ^[inferred] benchmark slug coined from paper since unnamed.

title: Six contextual vulnerability classes in agentic execution: harness hijacking, privacy leakage, unauthorized execution, supply-chain, tool abuse, encoding obfuscation
summary: DEEPTRAP enumerates six contextual risk classes for OpenClaw agents: harness hijacking (context steers agent toward attacker objectives, e.g. poisoned PLAYBOOK creating etc/cron.d/health_check), privacy leakage (most consistently activated, AGS up to 0.97), unauthorized execution, supply-chain compromise (via skills/packages/deps), tool abuse (trojan style checker embeds BLOG_API_KEY/CMS_TOKEN secrets into output), and encoding obfuscation. Across nine target models, Qwen3.5-Plus/DeepSeek-v4-Flash/Pro show high attack grading scores (AGS) with high utility grading (UGS), while Claude-Sonnet-4.6 shows lower AGS, indicating stronger resistance to contextual attacks.
notes: Results: privacy leakage most-activated; harness-hijack/encoding-obfuscation highly effective; Claude-Sonnet-4.6 most resistant. Iteration raises AGS from 0.65 to 0.75 over 5 rounds.

title: Hierarchical LLM-planner + RL-controller red teaming sustains multi-stage kill-chain attacks where standalone LLMs fail
summary: A hybrid red-teaming agent decouples strategic planning (frozen LLM emitting MITRE ATT&CK-tactic intent every 20 steps) from tactical execution (PPO RL controller acting every step over a 10-action ATT&CK-aligned space), with 4-layer kill-chain-aligned reward shaping (environment, milestone, constraint, intent-alignment) and optional Reflexion memory. Evaluated in CybORG CAGE 4 against an H-MARL Expert blue team over 500-step episodes. Standalone LLM agents (14 models, 0.6B-70B incl. Foundation-Sec-8B, DeepHat-7B, DeepSeek-R1) fail to sustain multi-stage campaigns due to long-horizon state-tracking and action-repetition limits; the hybrid architecture is needed for robust autonomous adversary emulation against AI-enabled SOAR defenders.
notes: Method = frozen LLM planner (intent every 20 steps) + PPO controller; reward shaping over 4 layers. Metrics = episode compromise rate (ECR), attack action count (AAC), avg host discovery (AHD).

title: Standalone LLM cyber agents underperform RL by ~5x reward and exhibit action-repetition loops in long-horizon ops
summary: Citing prior CAGE-4 evidence, the paper documents that all-LLM blue teams achieve mean rewards ~5x worse than all-RL teams (-2,547 vs -493) while operating at ~1/104th decision speed, struggle with precise state tracking over hundreds of sequential decisions, exhibit action-repetition loops, and cannot learn from trial-and-error within an operational context. Domain-specialized small models (Foundation-Sec-8B, CyberPal 2.0, DeepHat) narrow the gap via security fine-tuning (fine-tuning a base vs instruction-tuned model yields 2.7x larger gains), but RL-based offensive red-team agents remain under-explored (only ~8 of 160 surveyed agentic-security papers use RL). Motivates frozen-LLM-strategy + trainable-RL-tactics hybrids.
notes: Reward gap (-2,547 vs -493) and 8/160 RL stat are cited from prior work (evidence_grade B for those). Foundation-Sec-8B / DeepHat-7B are domain-specialized offensive models.

title: Multi-agent actor-critic LLM system classifies CVEs into Non-AI / AI-Supply-Chain / Adversarial-AI and maps to NIST AI 100-2e2025
summary: An actor-critic multi-agent system (CVE Classifier Agent + NISTAML Mapper Agent, each with classifier/mapper actor + critic reviewer sub-agents, GPT-4o-mini, capped at 3 loops) classifies CVEs into Non-AI, AI Supply Chain, and Adversarial AI, then maps Adversarial-AI CVEs to the NIST AI 100-2e2025 (NISTAML) adversarial-ML taxonomy (Availability/Integrity/Privacy/Misuse Violations + Supply-Chain Attacks). On a stratified validation sample, accuracy is 76.6% (Adversarial-AI recall 1.0 / precision 0.524; Non-AI precision 1.0 / recall 0.775). The pipeline operationalizes mapping unstructured CVE descriptions to a standards taxonomy via LLM judges.
notes: Method = actor-critic multi-agent (Google ADK, GPT-4o-mini). Datasets = ~128k CVEs (2021-2025), NISTAML taxonomy. Validation via Cochran stratified sample, confusion matrix.

title: Adversarial-AI share of AI CVEs grew from 0% (2021) to ~50% (2025); many NISTAML subcategories empty/under-reported
summary: Of ~128,000 CVEs (2021-2025), ~1.57% are AI-relevant: ~1.05% AI Supply Chain and ~0.52% Adversarial AI. AI Supply Chain dominated early (100% of AI CVEs in Q1 2021) but Adversarial AI's quarterly share rose steadily, exceeding supply-chain in Q2 2024 / Q1 2025 (reaching ~47.5-55%). Within Adversarial AI, Integrity Violations (NISTAML.02) and Privacy Compromises (NISTAML.03, esp. .036 Leaking Information from User) dominate; Misuse and Supply-Chain-Attacks (NISTAML.05, <3%) are lowest. Several subcategories (Clean-label/Data Poisoning .012/.013, Indirect Prompt Injection .015/.016) have zero CVEs, signalling under-research or under-reporting of adversarial-AI attack vectors.
notes: Empty subcategories = NISTAML.012/.013/.015/.016 = coverage gap signal for standards analyst. Membership-inference / model-extraction may be 'shadow CVEs' / security-by-obscurity.

title: Comiter taxonomy: AI attacks split into input attacks and poisoning attacks, exploiting inherent ML limitations not code bugs
summary: The Belfer report defines an 'AI attack' as adversarial manipulation exploiting inherent limitations of ML algorithms (not fixable code bugs), dividing attacks into input attacks (perturbing inputs at inference, e.g. tape on a stop sign making a self-driving car see a green light; imperceptible digital perturbations) and poisoning attacks (corrupting training data or model to install backdoors triggerable at the attacker's chosen time/place). It argues AI attacks expand the cyberattack surface to physical objects and data, require no traditional 'hacking' or even a computer, and cannot be solved with existing cybersecurity toolkits, constituting a distinct new vertical of vulnerability with offensive-weaponization potential.
notes: 2019 policy report (evidence_grade C = opinion/policy synthesis). Input attack = evasion/adversarial-example; poisoning attack = backdoor. Foundational framing for later AML threat taxonomies.

title: AI Security Compliance: PCI-style mandated programs across planning, implementation, and mitigation stages
summary: Comiter proposes 'AI Security Compliance' programs modeled on PCI compliance for payments, to reduce attack risk and impact by driving best-practice adoption: considering attack risks/surfaces when deploying AI, adopting IT-reforms that raise attack cost, and creating attack-response plans. Requirements span three lifecycle stages (planning, implementation, mitigation) and five most-affected sectors (content filters, military, law enforcement, commercial AI-fication of human tasks, civil society). Regulators should mandate compliance for government use and as a pre-condition for selling AI to government, mandatory for high-risk private uses and optional for low-risk uses to avoid stifling innovation. An early precursor to NIST AI RMF / EU AI Act risk-tiered governance.
notes: ^[inferred] linkage to NIST AI RMF / EU AI Act as later realizations of the risk-tiered mandate idea (report predates both).

title: AI security is an enabling requirement, not a standalone ethics principle, and can conflict with explainability/privacy
summary: Surveying AI ethics guides (Asilomar, UNESCO, Montreal, IEEE EAD, EU HLEG, AI4People), security is rarely a standalone principle but a necessary-but-not-sufficient enabler subsumed under non-maleficence and privacy. The paper argues this oversimplifies: stronger security can trade off against explainability (XAI methods increase attack susceptibility) and exploiting an AI vulnerability can be ethically justified (e.g. anti-surveillance facial-recognition evasion via adversarial accessories, or Nightshade data poisoning to protect copyright). Security viewed as a deployer obligation to those affected, vs the deployer's CIA-of-own-assets lens, can diverge across stakeholders.
standards: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
EU HLEG Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI
notes: Nightshade = prompt-specific poisoning against text-to-image models reframed as a defensive tool. Dual-use framing: vulnerability exploitation can be ethically legitimate.

title: Searching six incident repositories yields only ~6 fully-relevant AI-vulnerability incidents, exposing cataloguing gaps
summary: Applying a four-criteria '4I' relevance scheme (Incident, Intrusion, Impact, Intelligence) to six repositories (AIAAIC ~1400, AIID ~650, AVID <50, Where in the World is AI?, CISA KEV, EuRepoC), only 6 incidents fully satisfy all criteria (~27 partial, ~8 possible). Fully-relevant cases: Tay poisoning, Facebook COVID fact-check evasion, remoteli.io bot prompt-injection hijack, TikTok suicide-video moderation evasion, Chinese tax-system facial-recognition camera-hijack ($77M fraud), and PyTorch dependency-chain compromise. AVID conflates vulnerabilities/reports with placeholder text; KEV and EuRepoC yielded zero AI-relevant hits. The small count reflects definitional ambiguity of 'AI vulnerability', inconsistent reporting, under-disclosure, and keyword-search limits, so real-world impact of AI vulns cannot yet be reliably gauged.
notes: Search Nov 2023. remoteli.io = prompt-injection-to-arbitrary-instruction; PyTorch chain = supply-chain dependency poisoning; tax-system = facial-recognition spoof for access control. KEV/EuRepoC zero AI hits = traditional-DB blind spot.

title: Ollama 'Probllama' RCE via unvalidated model-pull digest path traversal (CVE-2024-37032)
description: Ollama before 0.1.34 does not validate the format of the digest (sha256 with 64 hex digits) when getting the model path, mishandling cases such as fewer/more than 64 hex digits or an initial ../ substring. A crafted OCI manifest pulled from a rogue registry lets an attacker write arbitrary files (e.g. /etc/ld.so.preload) via the /api/pull endpoint, yielding remote code execution on the inference host.

title: Ollama Zip-Slip RCE via directory traversal in GGUF zip import (CVE-2024-7773)
description: Ollama 0.1.37's parseFromZipFile function in server/model.go does not check for directory-traversal sequences (../) in filenames inside an imported zip archive, allowing an attacker to write arbitrary files and achieve remote code execution.

title: vLLM memory corruption / RCE via unsafe prompt-embedding tensor deserialization (CVE-2025-62164)
description: In vLLM 0.10.2 to before 0.11.1 the Completions API loads user-supplied serialized prompt-embedding tensors with torch.load() without sufficient validation. Because PyTorch 2.8.0 disables sparse-tensor integrity checks by default, a maliciously crafted tensor bypasses bounds checks and triggers an out-of-bounds write during to_dense(), leading to denial-of-service and potentially RCE in the unauthenticated, network-exposed inference server.

title: PyTorch torch.load RCE despite weights_only=True (CVE-2025-32434)
description: PyTorch <= 2.5.1 contains a remote code execution vulnerability when loading a model with torch.load(weights_only=True). The legacy deserialization code path was not fully disabled under weights_only=True, so a crafted model file can still execute arbitrary Python during unpickling. This undermines the primary defense the ML ecosystem relied on for untrusted model loading. Patched in 2.6.0.

title: HuggingFace Transformers arbitrary code execution via pickle in load_repo_checkpoint (CVE-2024-3568)
description: huggingface/transformers allows arbitrary code execution through deserialization of untrusted data in the load_repo_checkpoint() function of TFPreTrainedModel. A malicious serialized payload embedded in a checkpoint file is unpickled during checkpoint loading, executing attacker-controlled code in the model-loading process.

title: Keras Model.load_model arbitrary code execution even with safe_mode=True (CVE-2025-1550)
description: Keras Model.load_model permits arbitrary code execution, even with safe_mode=True, through a manually constructed malicious .keras archive. The config in the archive can be crafted to invoke arbitrary callables on load, bypassing the safe-mode mitigation introduced to block Lambda-layer code execution.

title: TensorFlow/Keras unsafe YAML deserialization RCE in model_from_yaml (CVE-2021-37678)
description: TensorFlow and Keras can be tricked into arbitrary code execution when deserializing a Keras model from YAML, because model_from_yaml uses yaml.unsafe_load. An attacker supplying a malicious model YAML achieves code execution on load.

title: LangChain 'LangGrinch' serialization-injection RCE / secret exfiltration (CVE-2025-68664)
description: Prior to LangChain core 0.3.81 and 1.2.5, the dumps()/dumpd() serialization functions do not escape free-form dictionaries containing 'lc' keys. Combined with the deserializer's trust of those keys, an attacker can inject a crafted object during (de)serialization to exfiltrate secrets or achieve remote code execution in LangChain-powered applications and agents.

title: LangChain JiraAPIWrapper arbitrary code execution via crafted input (CVE-2023-34540)
description: LangChain allows attackers to execute arbitrary code via crafted input passed to the JiraAPIWrapper component, which interpolates untrusted input into an evaluated expression. Part of a family of early LangChain chains/tools (LLMMathChain, APIChain) that reached eval()/exec() with model- or user-controlled content.

title: LlamaIndex arbitrary file read via path traversal in encode_image (CVE-2025-6209)
description: A path traversal vulnerability exists in run-llama/llama_index 0.12.27 to 0.12.40 in the encode_image function in generic_utils.py. By manipulating the image_path input an attacker reads arbitrary files on the server, including sensitive system files. Fixed in 0.12.41.

title: ComfyUI-Impact-Pack path traversal to arbitrary file write / RCE (CVE-2024-21575)
description: ComfyUI-Impact-Pack is vulnerable to path traversal due to missing validation of the image.filename field in a POST request to the /upload/temp endpoint, resulting in arbitrary file writes that may, under some conditions, lead to remote code execution on the ComfyUI server.

title: Flowise WriteFileTool/ReadFileTool unrestricted file path leading to file R/W and RCE (CVE-2025-61913)
description: In Flowise before 3.0.8 the WriteFileTool and ReadFileTool do not restrict file path access, allowing an authenticated attacker to read and write arbitrary files on the host, potentially leading to remote command execution in the low-code LLM-agent builder.

title: Flowise arbitrary code execution via crafted script to api/v1 (CVE-2024-31621)
description: Flowise prior to v1.8.1 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted script sent to the api/v1 component, an early auth/validation weakness in the agent-orchestration API surface.

title: mcp-remote OS command injection from malicious MCP server (CVE-2025-6514)
description: mcp-remote, a widely-used OAuth proxy connecting local MCP clients to remote MCP servers, is exposed to OS command injection when connecting to untrusted MCP servers: a crafted authorization_endpoint response URL is passed into the system shell, achieving remote code execution on the client. Affects 0.0.5 through 0.1.15. Demonstrates the MCP supply-chain trust problem where a malicious server compromises the client.

title: Serverless Framework MCP server command injection in list-projects tool (CVE-2025-69256)
description: A command injection vulnerability in the Serverless Framework built-in MCP server package (@serverless/mcp) arises from unsanitized input parameters passed to child_process.exec in the list-projects tool, enabling an attacker (via a malicious prompt/tool call) to inject arbitrary system commands on the host running the MCP server.

title: Ollama path-traversal file-existence disclosure in api/push (CVE-2024-39722)
description: Ollama before 0.1.46 exposes which files exist on the server via path traversal in the api/push route. An attacker can determine the presence of arbitrary files on the host, an information-disclosure primitive useful for chaining further attacks against the inference service.

title: AI-related flaws strain the CVE/CNA model: most are traditional CWEs in AI software, while prompt-injection-class flaws resist CVE assignment
summary: Empirical study of AI-related CVEs (Maugeri et al., ACM AISec '25) finds the overwhelming majority of disclosed AI vulnerabilities are conventional software weaknesses (CWE-502 unsafe deserialization, CWE-22 path traversal, CWE-78 OS command injection, CWE-94 code injection) sitting inside AI products such as LangChain, Ollama, vLLM, PyTorch, Keras, ComfyUI and MCP servers — not novel ML-specific defects. The CVE Program (MITRE as Primary CNA plus federated CNAs like GitHub, huntr.dev, JFrog, Snyk) handles these well, but model-level/behavioral flaws (prompt injection, jailbreak, training-data poisoning effects) sit awkwardly: they are often data/configuration-dependent, lack a fixed 'vulnerable version', and a 'patch' may be a probabilistic guardrail rather than a code fix, so CNAs frequently decline them. This is the reporting gap the platform tracks against continuous red teaming.
notes: CWE class distribution and product list ^[extracted] from NVD records confirmed in this cycle; the CNA-decline pattern for behavioral flaws is ^[inferred] from the OWASP-LLM debate and the cited study.

title: Whether prompt injection deserves a CVE: concrete app-level injections now get CVEs, but the architectural class does not
summary: Prompt injection is OWASP LLM01:2025 and maps to MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act and ISO/IEC 42001, yet its CVE status is contested. The emerging consensus in practice: a SPECIFIC, exploitable instance in a named product/version DOES warrant a CVE (e.g. indirect-injection-to-RCE chains in Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and serialization-injection chains like LangChain CVE-2025-68664), whereas prompt injection as an ARCHITECTURAL property of LLMs — present in essentially every model with no patchable 'fixed version' — does not fit CVE/CVSS semantics. CVSS itself is a poor fit for adversarial-ML severity (no notion of attack success rate, transferability, or guardrail bypass probability), motivating complementary schemes (ATLAS, AI incident databases, model/system cards) alongside CVE.
notes: OWASP LLM01:2025 ranking and framework mappings ^[extracted]; the 'instance-yes / class-no' CVE boundary and CVSS-unfitness argument are ^[inferred] synthesis across the OWASP debate, the CVSS-validity arXiv work, and the AISec '25 study.

title: AI vulnerability disclosure runs on federated CNAs and bug-bounty platforms, but coverage breaks down for model/data and agentic-supply-chain flaws
summary: AI flaws today flow through coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) and vendor disclosure programs (VDP) via the MITRE CVE Program's federated CNA model: GitHub Security Advisories, huntr.dev (AI/ML-focused bug bounty), JFrog, Snyk, and vendor CNAs mint most AI CVEs, mapped to CWEs and ATLAS. The model works for code-level vulns in AI infrastructure (deserialization, path traversal, command injection, SSRF) but breaks down on (a) model-supply-chain integrity (malicious models on Hugging Face, where the 'product' is data not code), (b) MCP/A2A agentic supply chain where trust crosses server boundaries with no shared identity, and (c) emergent/behavioral failures that have no version anchor. The platform's recommendation: pair CVE/CVD with continuous red teaming and an AI-incident register (AIID/OECD AIM) so behavioral and supply-chain risk that never becomes a CVE is still tracked and disclosed.
notes: CNA/bug-bounty routing (GitHub, huntr.dev, JFrog, Snyk) ^[extracted] from the CVE records collected this cycle; the three coverage-breakdown classes and the CVE+continuous-RT pairing recommendation are ^[inferred].

title: High volumes of low-quality, low-value vulnerability reports persistently burden CVD/BBP operators
summary: Qualitative study of 39 surveyed and 8 interviewed CVD operators finds that the dominant operational issue across both BBPs and VDPs is large volumes of duplicate, invalid, or low-severity reports that consume operator resources for little security benefit. The same fears and issues identified in earlier studies (Al-Banna 2018) persist, suggesting little systemic progress. Operators counter this with scope restriction (in/out-of-scope definitions), reward-only-valuable-reports policies, and managed/invite-only platform programmes.
notes: Triage-side of CVD/VDP. Survey is self-reported sentiment (Likert + thematic analysis), hence grade B. Standards ISO/IEC 30111 ^[inferred] as the response-handling complement to the disclosure standard cited.

title: Organisations use CVD report information to change security activities but rarely integrate it deeply into the SDLC
summary: A majority of surveyed organisations (22 of 38) reported that CVD-programme results prompted changes to security practices, most often security testing tools/methods, internal communication processes, and specification of security requirements. However, none integrated results to the depth of a full 'bug bounty lifecycle' (BBLC) feedback-to-SDLC loop; utilisation was shallow and reactive, attributed to lack of resources and lack of internal institutional change. Recommendations include defining internal report-routing pathways and communicating report patterns to relevant parties.
notes: Maps the 'feedback-to-SSDL' step. Data: closed-form + open-ended survey across BBP/Both/VDP programme types.

title: Automated LLM red teaming operationalizes an attacker/target/judge triad across TAP, PAIR, Crescendo, AutoDAN-Turbo, ReNeLLM, GPTFuzzer
summary: Primer compares state-of-the-art algorithmic red-teaming methods that automate jailbreak/prompt-injection discovery using an attacker LLM, a target LLM, and a judge/scorer LLM. TAP probes breadth-first with pruning; PAIR refines iteratively depth-first; Crescendo escalates toxicity multi-turn in black-box settings; ReNeLLM embeds disallowed intent via nested-scenario prompt rewriting; GPTFuzzer mutates seed jailbreak prompts; AutoDAN-Turbo autonomously discovers, stores, and evolves jailbreak strategies as a lifelong agent (>90% ASR on GPT-4-Turbo, >70% average-success gain over SOTA).
notes: Survey/primer (grade B) over primary methods; ASR figures are quoted secondhand from the original artifacts. ATLAS AML.T0054 (LLM jailbreak) ^[inferred] mapping.

title: Non-determinism of LLMs makes single LLM-as-judge evaluation unreliable; heterogeneous ensembles + human/rule fallback recommended
summary: The paper's central thesis: because LLMs are stochastic (autoregressive, probabilistic token sampling), using a single LLM as judge/scorer for red-team evaluation is a Catch-22 — the evaluator inherits the same non-determinism it is meant to assess. It recommends a consensus-plus-calibration model: ensembles of heterogeneous-architecture (transformer + state-space, e.g. Mamba) and differently-aligned (RLHF/constitutional/adversarial) judge LLMs, plus human-in-the-loop oversight and rule-based verification (keyword filters, symbolic checks) as conformance fallbacks, to reduce correlated bias and false consensus.
notes: Argument/opinion piece recommendation (grade C). Reliability concern echoes LLM-as-judge survey literature it cites.

title: Red teaming must be continuous (not one-time) and is especially critical for AI agents using LLMs as components
summary: The primer stresses that algorithmic red teaming is a mandate rather than a one-time exercise: as applications and models change, and as autonomous AI agents embed LLMs as components, a single failure can lead to significant public scrutiny. It frames proactive, continuous red teaming as the responsible-AI counterpart to safety/robustness/trustworthiness guardrails, and contemplates 'uncensored' models purpose-built for red-teaming to overcome target-model guardrails that block probes.
notes: Forward-looking framing/opinion (grade C). Agentic threat tags ^[inferred] from the paper's emphasis on LLM-component agents.

title: Frontier AI models can autonomously find and exploit production-software vulnerabilities, collapsing the find-vs-fix window
summary: Hathaway argues that frontier AI models (released April 2026) can autonomously discover and exploit vulnerabilities in production software at speed and depth that previously required expert human researchers, collapsing the time window from ~60 days to ~4 hours and exposing 40 years of accumulated 'field it fast, fix it later' technical debt. Because finding and fixing are separate workflows, the widening gap between them is where organisations are most vulnerable to a coming surge of exploitation against unpatched and legacy/unsupported systems.
notes: Senior-leader perspective / forward claim (grade C). Specific vendor claims (Anthropic Mythos 99% detection, China 360 agent ~1000 vulns) are reported as illustrative, treat as ^[ambiguous].

title: Responsible disclosure must shift from a reactive/fragmented process to coordinated national/international resilience with automated repair
summary: Drawing on the evolution from Trusted CMM and CVE to EO 14028 SBOMs, Hathaway argues responsible disclosure can no longer be a per-vendor, reactive process. She calls for governments and industry to map patch volume and surge capacity across strategic assets (GDP-at-risk, critical-citizen-services-at-risk, national-security risk), accelerate automated vulnerability repair (DARPA AIxCC), enforce vendor fiduciary remediation duties, and prepare emergency response (National Guard cyber units, tabletop exercises) for simultaneous high-severity incidents — invoking a Y2K-style coordinated mobilization.
notes: Policy recommendation (grade C). Captures the natsec-convergence and CVD standardization thesis. PRC mandatory vulnerability-reporting law (2021) cited as a contrasting regulatory model.

title: CSET proposes standardized key components for a federated mandatory AI incident reporting regime
summary: The brief synthesizes a standardized, high-level set of AI-incident reporting components from existing AI incident initiatives and from transportation/healthcare/cybersecurity practice. Components: type of event (incident vs near miss), harm dimensions (type/mechanism/severity), technical data (AI system card, model card, datasheet), context/circumstances/stakeholders, and post-incident data (incident response, ethical impact). Criteria are that components be easy, adaptable, and functional. Intended as a mandatory-reporting template that can also inform voluntary and citizen reporting.
notes: Policy synthesis brief (grade B). Builds on the authors' prior 'Hybrid AI Incident Reporting' framework (mandatory/voluntary/citizen). ISO/IEC 23894 ^[inferred] as the AI risk-management complement.

title: CSET adopts OECD AI incident/near-miss/hazard definitions and scopes mandatory reporting to incidents and near misses
summary: The brief adopts OECD definitions: an AI incident is an event where development/use/malfunction of AI directly or indirectly leads to harm (health, critical-infrastructure disruption, human-rights/legal violation, or property/community/environment harm); a near miss is the same but harm was averted by chance or interception; a hazard is an unsafe condition that could plausibly lead to such harm. It argues incidents and near misses warrant mandatory reporting (near misses reveal conditions that prevented harm), while hazards are better suited to voluntary reporting. Severity is nuanced/context-dependent; an AI-incident severity metric is left for future work.
notes: Definitional/taxonomic finding (grade B). Harm-dimension severity factors (remediability, distribution, exposed population, duration, optionality, frequency) align with the §6.1 harm/incident ontology. ISO 14971 ^[inferred] as the harm/severity analog from medical-device risk management.

title: Crescendo: benign multi-turn escalation referencing the model's own outputs defeats single-turn-tuned safety
summary: METHOD: Crescendo is a black-box multi-turn jailbreak that opens with an abstract, benign question and gradually intensifies across turns, leveraging the model's tendency to follow its own recently generated text (a 'foot-in-the-door' escalation). It uses no adversarial or optimized tokens, only normal API interaction with backtracking when refused. DATASETS: AdvBench subset (plus HarmBench for generalizability), 17 task categories. RESULTS: Manual Crescendo jailbreaks ChatGPT, Gemini Pro/Ultra, Claude-2/3, LLaMA-2/3 70b across nearly all tasks, and also jailbreaks multimodal image generation. Highlights that current benchmarks/alignment focus on single-turn attacks and are easily circumvented by multi-turn ones.
notes: Multi-turn threat model is the key contribution; single-turn benchmarks under-measure it.

title: Crescendomation automates multi-turn jailbreaking with a Judge / Secondary-Judge / Refusal-Judge LLM stack and backtracking
summary: METHOD: Crescendomation uses GPT-4 as the attacker and an LLM Judge to score task completion, a Secondary Judge to audit the Judge's reasoning and cut false positives, and a Refusal Judge that triggers backtracking (retract/edit the last turn, up to 10 retries) when a refusal or content filter fires. Success is also cross-checked with Azure Content Filter and Google Perspective API. DATASETS/RESULTS: On the AdvBench subset, Crescendomation beats MSJ, CIA, PAIR and CoA by 29-61% ASR on GPT-4 and 49-71% on Gemini-Pro. Demonstrates the multi-judge pattern needed to reliably evaluate stealthy multi-turn attacks.
notes: Layered LLM-judge design directly addresses false-positive/negative problem of automated red-team scoring.

title: AutoDAN-Turbo: a lifelong agent autonomously discovers and evolves a reusable jailbreak strategy library from scratch
summary: METHOD: A black-box framework with three modules: attack-generation/exploration (attacker LLM + target LLM + scorer LLM scoring 1-10), strategy-library construction (a summarizer LLM extracts named strategies from diffs between higher- and lower-scoring attack-log pairs and stores them as embedding-keyed (response, prompt, score-delta, strategy) records), and embedding-based strategy retrieval feeding the attacker. It needs no human-designed strategies or predefined scopes and supports plug-and-play injection of external strategies. RESULTS: On HarmBench it surpasses the runner-up Rainbow Teaming by 74.3% average ASR and 92.3% on StrongREJECT; 88.5 ASR on GPT-4-1106-turbo, rising to 93.4 with 7 injected human strategies; learned library transfers across target models.
notes: ICLR 2025 Spotlight. Lifelong-learning agent that accumulates an evolving attack-strategy memory is a step toward continuous automated red teaming.

title: An accumulating, transferable jailbreak-strategy library is a durable adversarial asset that outlives any single target
summary: METHOD/RESULT: AutoDAN-Turbo's summarizer LLM converts every score-increasing attack into a reusable, embedding-retrievable strategy; off-the-shelf mode fixes the library and replays it against new models/datasets, while continual mode keeps growing it. Experiments show off-the-shelf transfer is already highly effective across target models, meaning the offensive value compounds over time and is portable across attackers and victims. IMPLICATION for SE/agentic assurance: defenders face an adversary with persistent, growing memory; one-off model patching is insufficient, motivating continuous re-testing and library-aware defenses. Mirrors the agentic-SDLC concern that autonomous agents accumulate capability across runs.
notes: ^[inferred] The 'durable adversarial asset' framing is synthesized from the paper's transferability + lifelong-learning results.

title: ReNeLLM generalizes jailbreaks into prompt rewriting + scenario nesting, using the LLM itself as the attacker
summary: METHOD: ReNeLLM is an automatic, training-free framework that (1) rewrites a harmful prompt with six semantics-preserving functions (paraphrase-with-fewer-words, alter-sentence-structure, misspell-sensitive-words, insert-meaningless-chars, partial-translation, change-expression-style) to disguise intent, then (2) nests it inside one of three universal task scenarios (code completion, text continuation, table filling) to shift the model's attention. A harmfulness-evaluator LLM gates each step. DATASETS: Harmful Behaviors / AdvBench (520 prompts), classified into 7 scenarios. RESULTS: SOTA GPT-ASR (86.9 GPT-3.5, 58.9 GPT-4, 90.0 Claude-1, 69.6 Claude-2) vs much weaker GCG/AutoDAN/PAIR; ablation shows rewriting AND nesting are both required; time-per-sample cut 76.6% vs GCG and 86.2% vs AutoDAN.
notes: NAACL 2024. Code-completion nesting ties jailbreak risk to vulnerable-code-gen surface.

title: Generalized rewriting+nesting evades moderation/PPL/RA-LLM defenses by shifting attention off the malicious span
summary: METHOD/RESULT: ReNeLLM tests its prompts against OpenAI Moderation Endpoint, a perplexity (PPL) filter, and RA-LLM. Rewriting+nesting render the original malicious intent covert and shift model attention away from the harmful token spans, so OpenAI moderation gives ~0% ASR-reduction and PPL only -4.1%; only RA-LLM meaningfully reduces ASR (-28% Llama2, -24% Claude-2) but at a usability cost. RESULT on robustness: after ensembling six generated prompts, GPT-ASR approaches 100% across all categories, showing the security of one prompt does not imply security of its semantic variants. IMPLICATION: safety alignment and content filters must generalize over paraphrase/nesting transformations, not memorize surface forms.
notes: Defense-evasion measurements grade the robustness of common guardrails.

title: LLM-as-a-Judge: a formal definition and four-axis framework (what / use / improve / evaluate) for using LLMs as evaluators
summary: METHOD: The survey gives a formal definition E <- P_LLM(x (+) C) (and a reliability variant R <- f_R(P_LLM, x, C)) covering graders, evaluators, critics, verifiers, examiners and reward/ranking models. It organizes the field by how to USE a judge (in-context learning, model selection, post-processing, evaluation pipeline), how to IMPROVE it (prompt design, capability/fine-tuning, output optimization), and how to EVALUATE it (agreement with human judgment, bias, adversarial robustness, meta-evaluation). RESULT: proposes a dedicated meta-evaluation benchmark and a reliability-oriented research agenda. Directly grounds the LLM-judge scoring layer that red-team benchmarks (HarmBench/StrongREJECT/JailbreakBench) and automated attacks depend on.
notes: Survey (evidence-grade B). Anchors the evaluation/teaming taxonomy node llm-as-a-judge.

title: LLM judges carry biases and are adversarially manipulable, threatening the reliability of red-team success metrics
summary: METHOD/RESULT: The survey synthesizes evidence that LLM-as-a-Judge suffers systematic biases (position, verbosity, self-preference, etc.) and is vulnerable to adversarial manipulation of the evaluated content, so 'merely employing a judge does not ensure evaluations aligned with established standards.' It catalogues mitigation strategies (consistency/calibration, bias correction, secondary review) and stresses meta-evaluation and temporal consistency. IMPLICATION for RT platform: attack-success-rate and harm classifications produced by LLM judges are themselves an attack surface and a confidence-limiting factor; red-team pipelines should audit the judge (e.g., secondary-judge/refusal-judge designs) and treat judge reliability as a measured control, not an assumption.
notes: Judge reliability is a cross-cutting risk for every benchmark-driven finding in the corpus.

title: Manual adversarial 'red-teaming' of an assistant produces the HH harmlessness dataset that RLHF trains against
summary: METHOD: Anthropic collects two crowdworker datasets against 52B models: helpfulness (pick the more helpful response) and harmlessness, where workers adversarially probe / red-team the model to elicit harmful responses and pick the MORE harmful one (the released HH-RLHF data). Preference models are trained on the mixture and used as the RLHF reward, with an iterated 'online' weekly-cadence loop. RESULTS: PMs trained on only one objective do far worse on the other; mixed training yields models that are both helpful and much less harmful; purely-helpful RLHF models are far easier to red-team. Establishes human red-teaming as the data-generating process for harmlessness alignment.
notes: Foundational red-team-data + RLHF reference cited by much of the corpus.

title: Helpfulness/harmlessness tension eases with scale; OOD detection can reject strange/harmful requests with no harmful examples
summary: RESULT: There is a measurable tension between helpfulness and harmlessness at both the preference-model and RLHF-policy level, but larger preference models become robust to the helpful/harmless mix and perform better on both simultaneously. RLHF for HH carries little capability cost at 13B/52B (alignment bonuses on zero/few-shot NLP) and can be combined with specialized skills (summarization, code) without degradation. Out-of-distribution detection rejects most strange/harmful requests using essentially no harmful training examples, and RL reward relates ~linearly to sqrt(KL) from the initial policy. IMPLICATION: a residual-risk control (OOD rejection) and a scaling argument for why HH alignment need not trade off capability.
notes: OOD-detection rejection is a deployable harmlessness control.

title: Constitutional AI replaces human harm labels with AI self-critique + RLAIF steered by a short natural-language constitution
summary: METHOD: CAI has two stages. Supervised: a helpful-only model generates responses to red-teaming prompts, then critiques and revises them against principles randomly drawn from a constitution; the revised data fine-tunes the model. RL ('RLAIF'): the model generates response pairs to harmful prompts and an AI evaluator picks the more harmless per a constitutional principle, producing an AI preference dataset that trains a harmlessness preference model used as the RL reward. No human labels for harms are used. Chain-of-thought makes harm judgments more legible. RESULTS: RL-CAI is a Pareto improvement over standard RLHF on the harmlessness/helpfulness frontier and is non-evasive (explains objections instead of refusing); CoT-based AI harm identification becomes competitive with human-feedback PMs as scale grows.
notes: Anchors the future.constitutional-ai-teaming taxonomy node and AI-supervises-AI scaling direction.

title: AI-feedback scaled supervision foreshadows AI-auditor / AI-assurance agents but obscures decision-making
summary: RESULT/IMPLICATION: CAI demonstrates 'scaling supervision' - using capable AI to supervise other AIs - reducing human input to ~ten natural-language principles plus few-shot examples while improving reliability. CoT reasoning is used to keep AI harm decisions legible, since the authors note automating decision-making can otherwise obscure it. This is direct evidence for the future-teaming frontier where AI auditor / AI assurance agents and continuous, constitution-driven red teaming supervise model behavior; it also raises an assurance concern that delegating harm judgment to AI requires transparency controls (legible critiques, auditable constitutions) to remain trustworthy.
notes: ^[inferred] Mapping CAI to the ai-auditor/ai-assurance-agent future direction is synthesized; the transparency caveat is the authors' own.

title: Text-based LLM jailbreaks transfer to MLLMs regardless of image input
summary: METHOD: JailBreakV-28K pairs 20000 LLM-transfer text jailbreaks (Logic/Cognitive-Overload, PAP/Persuade, Template, GCG) with Nature/Noise/Stable-Diffusion/Blank images. DATASETS: RedTeam-2K (2000 queries, 16 safety policies) and JailBreakV-28K (28000 cases). RESULTS: across 10 open-source MLLMs, transferred LLM jailbreaks reach 50.5% avg ASR and 68.7% avg ASR on the underlying LLM text-encoders; the image (blank/noise/natural) barely changes ASR (coefficient of variation 9.0), proving the jailbreak is driven by text, so MLLMs inherit textual vulnerabilities from their LLM backbone.
notes: Measured ASR over 10 MLLMs; benchmark introduced by the paper.

title: MLLMs are most vulnerable to jailbreaks on economic-harm and malware safety policies
summary: RESULTS: per-policy ASR analysis on JailBreakV-28K shows the highest vulnerability under 'Malware' (57.9% avg ASR) and 'Economic Harm/Health' (53.1% avg ASR) safety policies across the 10 evaluated MLLMs. This concentrates risk on cyber- and finance-adjacent misuse and gives a benchmark-grounded prioritization signal for defense, indicating alignment effort is unevenly distributed across the 16 RedTeam-2K policy categories.
notes: Per-policy ASR measured.

title: Typographic visual prompts (FigStep) bypass LVLM safety because visual embeddings are not safety-aligned
summary: METHOD: FigStep rephrases a prohibited query into a numbered-list statement, renders it as a typographic image, and pairs it with a benign incitement text-prompt, transferring harmful content from the textual to the visual domain to evade the LLM's text-only safety alignment. DATASETS: SafeBench (500 harmful questions, 10 topics) and SafeBench-Tiny. RESULTS: 82.5% avg ASR across 6 open-source LVLMs (vs 44.8% vanilla) with low perplexity, jailbreaks GPT-4V/GPT-4o, and t-SNE shows typographic prompts make benign/prohibited embeddings non-separable; OCR-detection, random-noise, and system-prompt defenses all fail.
notes: Black-box; measured ASR over six LVLMs + GPT-4V/4o case study.

title: Benign step-by-step incitement plus embedded text is necessary for the multimodal jailbreak to succeed
summary: METHOD/RESULTS: FigStep ablation (SafeBench-Tiny) shows neither the typographic image alone (image-only query Q3' near 0-34% ASR) nor a benign text prompt alone jailbreaks the model; only embedding the unsafe words in the image AND providing a benign incitement text that triggers a step-by-step continuation yields the 82-92% ASR. FigStep(adv) and a red-teaming variant push MiniGPT4 to 100% ASR on Illegal Activity. This isolates the mechanism: safety guardrails ignore content in visual embeddings, while continuation-style benign prompts avoid triggering the textual safety filter.
notes: Ablation-grounded mechanism claim.

title: Unsafe-content rate rises ~3x as language resource availability decreases (unintentional multilingual jailbreak)
summary: METHOD: MultiJail translates English harmful prompts into 9 non-English languages (high/medium/low resource) and measures unsafe rate on ChatGPT and GPT-4 with GPT-4-as-evaluator (Cohen kappa 0.86 vs human). DATASETS: MultiJail (3150 samples). RESULTS unintentional scenario: ChatGPT unsafe rate rises from 4.34% (high-resource) to 14.92% (low-resource), GPT-4 from 3.60% to 10.16% — about 3x more harmful content for low-resource speakers, with Bengali alone reaching 28.25% (ChatGPT). Demonstrates safety training fails to generalize beyond English.
notes: First multilingual jailbreak dataset; measured unsafe rates.

title: Intentional multilingual adaptive attacks reach ~100% (ChatGPT) / 79% (GPT-4) unsafe output
summary: METHOD: combine a translated harmful prompt with an English malicious instruction (AIM from jailbreakchat), and adaptively select the best of a candidate language pool. RESULTS (MultiJail, intentional): combining multilingual prompts with malicious instructions raises ChatGPT to 80.92% and GPT-4 to 40.71%; the multilingual adaptive attack reaches 99.37% (ChatGPT) and 79.05% (GPT-4) unsafe. Machine translation suffices (11.15% vs 10.19% unintentional), so the attack needs no native speakers. Self-Defence fine-tuning cuts intentional unsafe from 80.92% to 60.00%.
notes: Adaptive multilingual attack + Self-Defence mitigation both measured.

title: Translating prompts into low-resource languages jailbreaks GPT-4 at 79% with no adversarial prompt
summary: METHOD: translate AdvBench unsafe English instructions into low-resource languages via Google Translate, query GPT-4, translate responses back. DATASETS: AdvBench Harmful Behaviors (520 prompts) over 12 languages. RESULTS: low-resource combined attacks bypass GPT-4's guardrail 79.04% of the time (vs <1% English; Zulu 53%, Scots Gaelic 43%), on par with gradient-based SOTA (~47% on older GPT-4); high/mid-resource languages stay <15%. Cost ~USD 0.02/1000 chars. Top topics: terrorism, financial manipulation, misinformation. Mechanism: mismatched generalization of English-centric safety training.
notes: Low-cost translation attack; measured BYPASS rate on AdvBench.

title: PoisonedRAG corrupts RAG knowledge bases to force attacker-chosen answers at up to 97% ASR with 5 injected texts
summary: METHOD: PoisonedRAG frames knowledge corruption as an optimization with a retrieval condition + a generation condition, crafting each malicious text P = S + I (S secures retrieval via the target question, I induces the target answer via an LLM); solved black-box and white-box (HotFlip). DATASETS: Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MS-MARCO (knowledge bases of 2.68M / 5.23M / 8.84M texts). RESULTS: injecting only 5 malicious texts per target question yields up to 97% (NQ), 99% (HotpotQA), 91% (MS-MARCO) ASR across 8 LLMs (PaLM2, GPT-3.5/4, LLaMA-2, Vicuna), beating prompt-injection, corpus-poisoning, and GCG baselines (~2 queries, <1s per text). Paraphrasing and perplexity defenses fail.
notes: First knowledge-corruption attack on RAG; ASR measured across 3 datasets x 8 LLMs.

title: Existing RAG defenses (paraphrasing, perplexity filtering) are insufficient against knowledge-base poisoning
summary: RESULTS: PoisonedRAG's two-part malicious text (S+I) is semantically coherent and low-perplexity, so paraphrasing- and perplexity-based detection defenses do not reliably remove it; ASR stays high under these defenses. Because the attacker only needs to inject a handful of texts (e.g., by maliciously editing ~6.5% of Wikipedia pages per a cited study, or posting fake content scraped into the KB), and the retrieval+generation conditions are jointly satisfied, the paper concludes new defenses are needed for retrieval-augmented systems in safety-critical domains (healthcare, finance, legal).
notes: Defense-evasion measured against paraphrasing/perplexity baselines.

title: Multimodal RAG is poisonable: targeted injection steers answers (56% ASR) and one untargeted entry collapses accuracy to 0%
summary: METHOD: MM-PoisonRAG injects adversarial image-text entries into a multimodal KB. Localized Poisoning Attack (LPA) crafts a query-specific factually-incorrect entry (caption via GPT-4 + Stable-Diffusion image; white-box LPA-Rt optimizes the image embedding toward the query via CLIP). Globalized Poisoning Attack (GPA) injects one untargeted entry whose embedding is pushed to the query cluster centroid and trains the reranker/generator toward 'Yes'/'sorry'. DATASETS: MultimodalQA, WebQA. RESULTS: LPA reaches up to 56% poisoned-answer accuracy (88.8% poisoned-retrieval recall) even black-box; GPA drives generation to 1.6% (MMQA) / 0% (WebQA) accuracy with a single injection.
notes: First multimodal-RAG poisoning framework; LPA/GPA ASR measured.

title: Multimodal-RAG poisoning transfers across retrievers and evades auditing/paraphrase defenses
summary: RESULTS: LPA-Rt adversarial entries optimized only against CLIP transfer to OpenCLIP and SigLIP retrievers, still halving true-context recall and doubling poisoned-answer accuracy (e.g., 45.6%/22.4% retrieval/accuracy drops on OpenCLIP) — so an attacker can weaponize an open-source surrogate to poison restricted closed-source multimodal RAG. Detection/defense evaluation (MultimodalQA/WebQA): CLIP-based auditing detects 0% of all four attack settings; abnormality detection catches only 7.2-10.4%; paraphrase- and feature-squeezing defenses leave attack potency essentially unchanged, exposing a defense gap for multimodal retrieval security.
notes: Transferability + defense-evasion measured (0% auditing detection).

title: Circuit breakers (Representation Rerouting) give attack-agnostic robustness by controlling harmful representations rather than patching attacks
summary: METHOD: Representation Rerouting (RR), a RepE/LoRA finetune, reroutes internal representations of harmful processes toward orthogonal/incoherent directions so generation 'short-circuits' when harmful content begins — independent of which input elicited it, so it generalizes to unseen attacks without adversarial training or I/O guard models. DATASETS: HarmBench attack suite (GCG, PAIR, TAP-T, AutoDAN, prefilling, input-embedding, RepE attack, multilingual), MT-Bench/OpenLLM for capability. RESULTS: average attack success rate cut from 76.7→9.8 (Mistral-7B) and 38.1→3.8 (Llama-3-8B), with the Cygnet variant ~0.8 avg ASR (~two orders of magnitude reduction), while MT-Bench/MMLU drop <1%. This is a defender-side teaming primitive: a guardrail that acts in latent space and can be paired with monitoring.
notes: Foundational RepE defense; measured ASR/capability results. ^[inferred] 'attack-agnostic' is the authors' framing, later contested by obfuscated-activations work [[find-obfuscated-activations-bypass-latent-defenses-2412]].

title: Representation-level circuit breakers extend defense to multimodal image hijacks and harmful agent function calls
summary: METHOD: same RR circuit-breaking loss applied to a multimodal model (LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B) and to an AI agent making function calls, with synthetic multimodal/function-calling circuit-breaker and retain sets. DATASETS: HarmBench + MM-SafetyBench (133 multimodal behaviors) under PGD image attacks; a 100-request harmful-function-call set + Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL). RESULTS: under white-box PGD, RR reduces multimodal compliance by 84% vs original and 85% vs safety-prompt, with MMMU/LLaVA-Wild within 0.5%; for agents, harmful function-call compliance drops 84% (no-attack) and 83% (forced calls) while BFCL is preserved. Shows latent-space defenses transfer across modalities where standalone adversarial robustness (image classifiers) still fails.
notes: Agent/multimodal extension of circuit breakers.

title: RMU machine unlearning removes WMDP hazardous (bio/cyber) knowledge while preserving general capability and resisting probes
summary: METHOD: Representation Misdirection for Unlearning (RMU) — a two-loss RepE finetune that scales up activation norm on hazardous (forget) data toward a random direction while an L2 retain loss preserves benign activations, updating only a few layers. DATASETS: WMDP (3,668 expert MCQs across bio/cyber/chem, $200K to build, ITAR/EAR-filtered) as forget-measurement; MMLU + MT-Bench as utility; forget corpora from PubMed/GitHub crawls. RESULTS: on Zephyr-7B, WMDP-Bio 63.7→31.2 and WMDP-Cyber 44.0→28.2 (near 25% random) while MMLU 58.1→57.1 and MT-Bench 7.33→7.10; linear probes on unlearned models recover little above chance — i.e. unlearning is a stronger safety floor than refusal because jailbroken-but-unlearned models lack the knowledge. Defines machine unlearning as a safety control and ships the WMDP benchmark to measure it.
notes: Introduces both WMDP benchmark and RMU. Robustness to fine-tuning later challenged by [[find-tampering-reverses-unlearning-16-steps-2502]].

title: Obfuscation attacks bypass latent-space monitors (SAEs, probes, OOD) and transfer across monitor types
summary: METHOD: 'obfuscation attacks' jointly minimize a behavioral loss (jailbreak / SQL generation) and an obfuscation loss D(R(x)) that forces harmful activations to look benign to a target monitor, via embedding suffixes (white-box), gradient-free hard-prompt suffixes (gray-box, FLRT), data poisoning, or fine-tuning. DATASETS: UltraChat/XSTest benign + Circuit-Breakers harmful data on Llama-3-8B-Instruct; StrongREJECT for harm; recall@1%FPR for detection; SQL-database execution for utility. RESULTS: against probes scoring ~90%+ recall, obfuscation drives recall 100%→0% while keeping ~90% jailbreak rate; attacks transfer (optimizing vs a Gaussian OOD detector fools input probes); a defender retraining a monitor on obfuscated examples still gets bypassed after 70+ rounds. Limit: obfuscating vs SQL-detectors degrades correct-SQL rate — a behavior/obfuscation tradeoff. Directly probes failures of Circuit Breakers and LAT. This is an LLM-as-a-defender stress test showing harmfulness has no single compact latent signature.
notes: Major critique of latent-space guardrails and interpretability-based monitors; informs how red teams should evaluate (and red-team) the monitor itself.

title: State-of-the-art LLM unlearning can be reversed within ~16 fine-tuning steps; tampering attacks predict held-out input-space risk
summary: METHOD: pit 8 unlearning methods (RMU, RR, ELM, RepNoise, GradDiff, TAR, LAT, K-FADE) and 9 safety-tuned models against 5 input-space (GCG, AutoPrompt, BEAST, PAIR, human) and 6 model-tampering attacks (embedding/latent perturbation, pruning, benign/LoRA/full fine-tune) on WMDP-Bio. DATASETS: WMDP-Bio forget/retain (bio papers), Wikitext, MMLU/MT-Bench/AGIEval utility; StrongREJECT autograder for jailbreaks. RESULTS: (1) model robustness lives on a low-dimensional subspace — 3 PCs explain 89% of attack-success variance; (2) fine-tuning attacks recover unlearned WMDP knowledge — best adversarial fine-tune beats input-space attacks on 64/65 models and within ~16 steps (sometimes 1); (3) tampering-attack success conservatively over-estimates held-out / proprietary UK-AISI input-space attack success (predictiveness r 0.77→0.83). EVAL-SCIENCE CLAIM: input-output evals only lower-bound worst-case risk; open-weight risk requires tampering evals.
notes: Key eval-methodology result: open-weight evals must include weight/latent tampering. ^[inferred] AML mappings approximate (model-tampering ~ model poisoning/evasion).

title: LLM-as-a-judge adoption outpaces validity/reliability scrutiny across four core assumptions (measurement-theory lens)
summary: METHOD: position paper applying measurement theory (construct validity's 7 dimensions per Jacobs & Wallach; reliability per Adcock & Collier) to four assumptions behind LLM judges (LLJs): proxy-for-human, capable, scalable, cost-effective. DATASETS: qualitative review of the LLJ literature grounded in three applications — summarization (SummEval), data annotation, safety alignment. RESULTS/CLAIMS: convergent validity is undermined because human-judgment ground truth is itself inconsistently collected (SummEval fluency instructions vary across papers in scale and definition); face validity is high even when judges are wrong (unfaithful CoT rationales); discriminant validity fails (judges conflate fluency/relevance, and LLM safety judges misclassify up to 100% of harmful generations as harmless under small perturbations or injected artifacts); predictive validity is threatened by data contamination, competitive-benchmark gaming (Chatbot Arena flaws), self-enhancement bias and preference leakage. Calls for context-specific validation before deploying LLJs (incl. as safety guardrails).
notes: Position paper; normative not measured. Directly relevant to red-team pipelines using LLM judges/safety classifiers as the harm oracle.

title: LLM safety judges over-rely on surface cues: small perturbations or injected artifacts flip harmful generations to 'harmless'
summary: METHOD: synthesis of cited evidence (Eiras et al.; Chen & Goldfarb-Tarrant) within a measurement-theory critique of LLM safety judges (LLSJs) such as Llama Guard, ShieldGemma, Guardformer used as real-time guardrails. RESULTS: LLSJs are highly sensitive to distribution shift and adversarial manipulation — small output modifications can lead them to misclassify up to 100% of harmful generations as harmless, and injecting artifacts (e.g. appending an apology to an unsafe prompt) misleads them, revealing reliance on loosely-correlated statistical cues (e.g. refusal/politeness) rather than genuine harm understanding. IMPLICATION: this is a discriminant-validity failure and a direct attack surface — red teams must red-team the judge/guardrail, not just the target model, because a gameable harm oracle invalidates downstream safety benchmarks and online moderation.
notes: ^[inferred] 'content-safety' sector tag; secondary evidence aggregated by the position paper (grade B).

title: Jailbreak Distillation builds renewable safety benchmarks that resist saturation/contamination and beat static benchmarks
summary: METHOD: JBDistill runs off-the-shelf jailbreak attacks (single-turn: TAP, PAP, AutoDAN-Turbo, Adversarial Reasoning; multi-turn: ActorAttack, Red Queen, CCA, Speak Easy) over a small set of development models (Llama2-7B, Llama3.1-8B, Gemma2-9B, OLMo2-7B) to over-generate a candidate prompt pool from HarmBench seed goals, then selects an effective subset via RankBySuccess / BestPerGoal / CombinedSelection optimizing three benchmark desiderata: effectiveness (avg ASR), separability (CI non-overlap across models), diversity (versatility/coverage). DATASETS: HarmBench (200 seed goals, 7 categories); 13 held-out evaluation models incl. proprietary/reasoning/specialized; AdvPrefix judge. RESULTS: single-turn JBDistill reaches 81.8% effectiveness vs HarmBench 18.4 / WildJailbreaks 63.2, generalizes to 10/13 held-out models above dev-set average ASR, is stable under construction changes (Kendall-tau 0.89), shows no dev-family bias, and is re-runnable to produce fresh benchmarks — directly countering saturation and contamination. Complements (not replaces) red-teaming.
notes: Addresses benchmark saturation/contamination directly; HarmBench seed goals, AdvPrefix judge. StrongREJECT/JailbreakBench cited as comparison context.

name: Circuit breakers / Representation Rerouting (RepE latent-space guardrail)
RMU machine unlearning of hazardous (CBRN/cyber) knowledge
Model-tampering (latent + fine-tuning) evaluation as worst-case capability assurance
Renewable distilled safety benchmark (JBDistill) against saturation/contamination

title: Cybench: open CTF benchmark shows LM agents autonomously solve professional-level cyber tasks up to 11-min human FST
summary: METHOD: Cybench specifies 40 professional-level CTF tasks (crypto, web, rev, forensics, pwn, misc) from 4 recent (2022-2024) competitions in a Kali Linux container, with subtasks for gradated scoring and first-solve-time (FST) as an objective difficulty axis. DATASETS: Cybench (40 CTF tasks), with subtask decomposition. RESULTS: Evaluating 8 models x 4 agent scaffolds, the best unguided agents (Claude 3.5 Sonnet 17.5%, GPT-4o, o1-preview) solve complete tasks taking human teams up to 11 minutes; no agent solved any task with FST >11 min (hardest = 24h54m, 136x). Subtask guidance raises performance (o1-preview 46.8%). Agent scaffolding effects are model-dependent. Establishes the de-facto open-source cyber agent benchmark adopted by UK/US AISI and Anthropic system cards.
notes: Primary measured benchmark (grade A). FST-based difficulty is the key methodological contribution. ATLAS AML.T0040 (ML-enabled offensive cyber) ^[inferred] as closest technique for autonomous CTF solving.

title: Cybench is a dangerous-capability uplift evaluation: agentic offensive-cyber capability is measurable and rising but bounded by task difficulty
summary: METHOD: Cybench frames CTF success as a proxy for real-world cyber-offense capability (identifying/exploiting CVE-like vulnerabilities) and is explicitly motivated by the 2023 US Executive Order's call to quantify dual-use cyber risk for policymakers and model providers. DATASETS: Cybench. RESULTS: Capability is real (non-zero success on 73% of <=11-min-FST tasks) but sharply bounded - agents cannot make the multi-step cryptographic 'insights' that take expert humans hours. Train-test overlap is minimized by recency. Safety refusals occurred only for Claude 3 Opus / Claude 3.5 Sonnet and were defeated by a 'cybersecurity expert' framing prompt. Provides the evaluation infrastructure for frontier cyber-capability thresholds and CVD/responsible-scaling governance.
notes: Risk-management lens on the same benchmark. NIST AI RMF ^[inferred] as the governance frame for dangerous-capability evals; refusal-bypass via role framing is a notable safety finding.

title: BountyBench reveals an offense-defense imbalance: AI agents patch real-world vulnerabilities far better than they exploit them
summary: METHOD: BountyBench instantiates 25 real-world systems with 40 monetized bug bounties ($10-$30,485, 9 of OWASP Top 10) as Detect/Exploit/Patch tasks over evolving codebase snapshots, using a novel Detect Indicator (a valid exploit must succeed on the vulnerable snapshot and fail on patched snapshots) and dollar value as an economic-impact metric. DATASETS: BountyBench (25 systems, 40 bounties, 120 tasks). RESULTS: Commercial coding agents (Codex CLI o3-high/o4-mini, Claude Code) are strong defenders (Patch 87.5-90%) but weaker attackers (Exploit 32.5-57.5%); custom agents are more balanced (Exploit 17.5-67.5%, Patch 25-60%). Agents completed $81,067 of Patch and $9,700 of Detect bounties. Information level (zero-day -> CWE -> full report) is an effective difficulty modulator; performance rises monotonically with information.
notes: Primary measured (grade A). Offense-defense asymmetry and dollar-impact metric are the novel contributions. Detect Indicator addresses the gap in invariant-only success conditions.

title: Monetized bug-bounty awards give AI cyber-agent evaluations a real-world economic-impact metric for risk governance
summary: METHOD: BountyBench is the first benchmark to attach real dollar awards (from public bug-bounty programs) to AI-agent cyber tasks, capturing capabilities across evolving real-world systems rather than static snapshots, and spanning the full vulnerability lifecycle (Detect/Exploit/Patch). DATASETS: BountyBench bounties sourced from public programs (e.g., Huntr), 85% disclosed in 2024-25. RESULTS: Economic framing enables policymakers to reason about both defensive value (>$81K of patching completed) and offensive risk; the Exploit-side harm is acknowledged as harder to quantify. The benchmark grounds dual-use cyber-capability claims in market-validated severity, complementing CTF-style and CVE-style benchmarks and feeding responsible-disclosure / pre-deployment evaluation regimes.
notes: Governance/standards lens. ISO/IEC 29147 (disclosure) and NIST AI RMF ^[inferred] as the disclosure/governance frames the dollar metric feeds. Grade B as the economic-impact-to-real-harm link is interpretive.

title: VulnBot: multi-agent role specialization + Penetration Task Graph enables fully autonomous end-to-end pentesting with open-source LLMs
summary: METHOD: VulnBot decomposes pentesting into reconnaissance/scanning/exploitation phases handled by specialized agents (Planner, Memory Retriever w/ RAG, Generator, Executor, Summarizer), coordinated by a Penetration Task Graph (PTG, a DAG of task dependencies) with a Check-and-Reflection mechanism. It directly targets four diagnosed LLM pentest failure modes: context loss (42.36% of failures), bad command generation, no error-handling, and weak cross-phase reasoning. DATASETS: AUTOPENBENCH (33 tasks), AI-Pentest-Benchmark (real machines from Vulnhub). RESULTS: With Llama3.1-405B, 30.3% overall / 69.05% subtask completion on AUTOPENBENCH vs 9.09% (Llama3.1-405B) and 21.21% (GPT-4o) baselines; with RAG, VulnBot completes real-world machines end-to-end where GPT-4o/Llama could not without human help. Uses a role-playing jailbreak to bypass LLM usage policies.
notes: Primary measured (grade A). PTG-based long-horizon planning and the role-playing jailbreak to defeat safety policies are the key red-team-relevant contributions. Open-source models reaching real-world autonomy is the uplift signal.

title: Context loss is the dominant failure mode (42%) of autonomous LLM pentest agents, motivating memory/summarization scaffolds
summary: METHOD: An empirical analysis of 220 experiments classified failure causes for open-source LLM pentest agents (Llama3.3-70B, Llama3.1-405B) across reconnaissance/scanning/exploitation phases. DATASETS: 220-run failure-cause study + AUTOPENBENCH. RESULTS: Session context loss accounts for 86/203 = 42.36% of failures (agents forget earlier discoveries as context overflows), followed by failed tool/command-parameter errors (19.21% + 19.7%), deadlock operations (5.42%), and false output interpretation (8.87%). This grounds four design 'takeaways' - context length, command generation, error handling, and dynamic cross-phase reasoning - and justifies VulnBot's Summarizer + RAG Memory Retriever + PTG architecture as mitigations. Generalizes the agentic-SDLC assurance lesson that long-horizon tool-using agents fail primarily on state/memory management, not raw capability.
notes: Failure-mode taxonomy from measured runs (grade A). Cross-cutting agentic-SDLC assurance insight beyond pentesting specifically.

title: Backdooring LLMs needs a near-constant absolute number of poison documents (~250), independent of model/dataset size
summary: METHOD: Largest pretraining-poisoning study to date - dense transformers 600M-13B params trained from scratch on Chinchilla-optimal data (up to 260B tokens), with N in {100,250,500} poisoned documents implementing a denial-of-service (gibberish-on-trigger) backdoor, plus ablations on poison rate, per-batch density, ordering, and continued clean training. DATASETS: 72 pretrained models; Pythia checkpoints for resumed-training ablations; fine-tuning on Llama-3.1-8B and GPT-3.5-turbo. RESULTS: As few as 250 poisoned documents reliably backdoor all model sizes (600M-13B) despite the largest training on >20x more clean data - 250 poisons = only 0.00016% of 13B tokens. Attack success is governed by ABSOLUTE poison count, not percentage; per-batch density/ordering matter little; continued clean training partially degrades backdoors. Same dynamics hold for fine-tuning. Implies poisoning gets EASIER, not harder, as models scale.
notes: Primary measured, high-novelty result (grade A) from UK AISI + Anthropic. ATLAS AML.T0020 (Poison Training Data) and AML.T0018 (Backdoor ML Model) are direct mappings. Threat to model supply chain / training-data integrity.

title: Training-data and fine-tuning poisoning yield covert backdoors that preserve clean capabilities and evade percentage-based defenses
summary: METHOD: The same study measures clean accuracy (CA) and near-trigger accuracy (NTA) for poisoned models and tests multiple backdoor objectives (denial-of-service gibberish, language-switch, harmful-compliance via fine-tuning on StrongReject-derived data). DATASETS: Pretrained 600M-13B models; Llama-3.1-8B and GPT-3.5-turbo fine-tuned with poisoned safety data. RESULTS: Poisoned models retain high CA/NTA - they behave normally without the trigger, so capability benchmarks do not reveal the backdoor; fine-tuning poisoning makes models comply with harmful requests only when the trigger is present, defeating safety training. Because attack success depends on absolute count, defenses framed around a low poisoning PERCENTAGE provide a false sense of security as datasets grow. Recommends data filtering + post-hoc backdoor detection/elicitation as defenses. Directly informs model-supply-chain risk and CVD for trained-model artifacts.
notes: Stealth/defense lens on the poisoning result. ISO/IEC 42001 ^[inferred] as the AI-management-system frame for supply-chain controls. StrongReject used as the harmful-QA source for fine-tuning experiments.

title: Prompt Infection: a single injected document self-replicates LLM-to-LLM across a multi-agent system like a worm
summary: METHOD: Prompt Infection introduces a self-replicating LLM-to-LLM injection composed of Prompt Hijacking + Payload + shared Data note + Self-Replication; a single infected external document (PDF/email/web) compromises the first agent which then propagates the prompt downstream. Evaluated on multi-agent apps (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo) over email/PDF/web tools under global vs local messaging, plus a 'society of agents' simulation (10-50 agents). DATASETS: 120 user instructions x 3 tool types (360 pairs) + agent-society simulation. RESULTS: MAS are highly susceptible; self-replication is the ONLY scalable method to compromise >2 agents under local messaging (where non-replicating injection cannot). Infection spreads logistically and scales faster in larger populations. Enables data theft (multi-agent cooperation: reader->DB->coder POST-exfiltration), scams, malware spread, and disinformation. Stronger models resist injection but execute attacks more effectively once compromised.
notes: Primary measured (grade A). Self-replication / 'AI worm' across agents is the novel threat class. ATLAS AML.T0051 (LLM Prompt Injection) + .001 (Indirect) map the injection vector. A2A/multi-agent-governance teaming nodes flag the defense frontier.

title: Stronger LLMs are not inherently safer in multi-agent systems: better injection resistance is offset by more capable attack execution
summary: METHOD: Failure-mode analysis of GPT-4o vs GPT-3.5-turbo under self-replicating and non-replicating Prompt Infection, plus an ablation showing the infection prompt can manipulate the memory importance-scoring model to persist in episodic memory. DATASETS: 360 instruction/attack pairs; memory-manipulation ablation (100 runs). RESULTS: GPT-4o ignores 66% of self-replicating attacks (vs 9% for GPT-3.5) - more robust at recognizing injections - but once compromised it executes malicious tasks more correctly (fewer 'deformed infection' / 'no action' failures), making it a more formidable attacker. Manipulated infection prompts get rated importance 10/10 (vs 1.94 unmanipulated), creating a self-amplifying persistence loop. Proposed LLM Tagging defense works only when combined with other safeguards. Conclusion: MAS safety assessments must account for downstream consequence-given-compromise, not just attack resistance.
notes: Stronger-not-safer + memory-poisoning persistence are the key risk insights. LLM Tagging is the defensive control (llm-as-a-defender). Grade A from measured failure-mode breakdown.

title: MCPTox: tool poisoning via MCP metadata achieves up to 72.8% ASR on real-world servers, defeating content-based safety alignment
summary: METHOD: MCPTox is the first benchmark for Tool Poisoning Attacks (TPA) in real MCP settings - malicious instructions embedded in a tool's metadata/description injected at MCP registration, where the malicious action is executed by a LEGITIMATE tool (the poisoned tool never runs, bypassing permission models). Built on 45 live MCP servers + 353 authentic tools, 1,312 test cases across 3 paradigms (Explicit/Implicit-Trigger Function Hijacking, Implicit-Trigger Parameter Tampering) over 11 risk categories. DATASETS: MCPTox (1,312 cases, 45 servers, 353 tools). RESULTS: 20 agents evaluated; average ASR 36.5%, up to 72.8% (o1-mini), 70.2% (Phi-4). Inverse scaling: more capable / reasoning-enabled models are MORE vulnerable (better instruction-following => more compliant with poisoned descriptions). Parameter Tampering is the most effective paradigm (46.7%). Content-based safety alignment is ineffective - max refusal <3% (Claude-3.7-Sonnet). Adapted IPI payloads (InjecAgent) drop to ~0% ASR, proving TPA needs a dedicated benchmark.
notes: Primary measured (grade A). MCP tool-poisoning depth + inverse-scaling + legitimate-tool-executes-payload (permission-model bypass) are the novel contributions. ATLAS AML.T0051(.001) map indirect injection via tool metadata.

title: MCP tool poisoning bypasses permission models because the payload is carried by a trusted legitimate tool, and reasoning amplifies risk
summary: METHOD: MCPTox's design principle requires each poisoned tool description to contain a Trigger Condition + Malicious Action + Plausible Justification, with the malicious action executed by an already-trusted legitimate tool on the server (never the poisoned tool itself). Q1-Q4 analysis ablates model scale/reasoning, attack paradigm, enhanced hijacking prompts, and defense behavior. DATASETS: MCPTox; Qwen3 reasoning on/off ablation; failure-mode/refusal analysis. RESULTS: Because calls to legitimate tools are less suspicious and evade new-untrusted-tool permission gates, agents are 'manipulated into' high-privilege actions (e.g., reading ~/.ssh/id_rsa as a 'security check'). Enabling reasoning raised Qwen3 average ASR by 27.8% (inverse scaling). The dominant failure was 'Ignored', but 18.9% of failures were 'Direct Execution' (still risky). This exposes a pre-execution trust gap in MCP/A2A agent protocols that runtime content filters cannot close - a first-class agentic-SDLC and protocol-security finding.
notes: Protocol-security/agentic-SDLC lens. Permission-model bypass via trusted-tool execution + inverse scaling are the load-bearing insights. ISO/IEC 42001 ^[inferred] as the control frame; flags MCP/A2A pre-execution trust as a standards gap.

title: Defense-industry CEO publicly calls for ban on fully autonomous AI weapons
description: The CEO of a major defense manufacturer (Rheinmetall) publicly urged global regulation banning lethal autonomous weapon systems that select and engage targets without meaningful human control, citing escalation and accountability risks. Reported on the OECD AI Incidents Monitor as a governance/safety hazard signal.

title: Cluster of AI deepfake defamation incidents targeting public figures
description: Multiple incidents in the same window: AI-generated fake images falsely depicting an Iranian footballer; a deepfake portraying a German football fan as Hitler; and a court order won by broadcaster Graham Norton against a platform over AI-generated deepfakes and false claims. Common pattern: generative image/video used for reputational and psychological harm against identifiable individuals.

title: Deepfake celebrity scam ads defraud consumers
description: A South Korean actress was targeted by deepfake AI scam advertisements promoting fraudulent products, using her likeness without consent. Part of a broader pattern of AI-generated celebrity-endorsement scam ads causing consumer financial loss and reputational harm.

title: AI-driven ad systems linked to scams targeting seniors and child harm
description: A major social platform's (Meta) AI-driven advertising and recommendation systems were reported to spread scams defrauding elderly users and to be linked to child-safety harms. Highlights misuse and excessive-agency risks in deployed recommender/ad-targeting AI.

title: Government deployment of real-time AI facial recognition surveillance
description: Western Australia Police deployed real-time facial recognition cameras to identify suspects in public spaces, and Kansas City planned AI facial recognition on public buses. Both raised privacy and civil-rights concerns over mass biometric surveillance without clear consent or oversight.

title: Autonomous robotaxi fleet recall over navigation/perception flaw
description: Waymo recalled nearly 4,000 robotaxis after AI-driven vehicles failed to correctly recognize closed freeway construction zones, creating physical-injury risk. A real-world autonomous-perception failure in deployed self-driving fleets.

title: AI-generated legal brief with fabricated citations triggers lawyer investigation
description: A Turkish lawyer was investigated after submitting an AI-generated legal brief containing incorrect/fabricated case citations. Continues the well-documented pattern (cf. Mata v. Avianca) of LLM hallucinated case law causing professional and judicial harm.

title: AI music generators sued over training on copyrighted songs
description: AI music-generation companies faced lawsuits (including from Australian artists) for training models on millions of copyrighted songs without permission. Economic/IP harm from unlicensed training-data acquisition.

title: National program to develop autonomous military AI defense systems
description: Morocco entered a strategic partnership to develop autonomous military AI defense systems. Flagged as a proliferation/escalation hazard for lethal autonomous systems with potential physical and national-security harm.

title: Warnings of existential strategic AI dependency on foreign providers
description: Analysts warned Europe of existential dependency on US AI firms for critical AI infrastructure, framing concentration of frontier-AI supply as a strategic/economic systemic risk. A governance-level hazard rather than a single technical failure.

title: Public-sector AI deployment raises union job-security concerns
description: France Travail's AI deployment prompted union concerns over job losses and degraded employment quality from automation of public-employment services. Socioeconomic harm signal (MIT subdomain 6.2).

title: Commercial face/gender classifiers fail far more on darker-skinned women
summary: Gender Shades audited IBM, Microsoft and Face++ gender classifiers and found error rates up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women vs 0.8% for lighter-skinned men - a ~34-point intersectional accuracy gap that drives downstream allocative and representational harm.

title: LLM and ML hiring tools reproduce demographic bias and fail the four-fifths rule
summary: Amazon scrapped a resume-screener that penalized 'women's' and all-women's-college graduates (Reuters 2018); a 2024 Bloomberg audit found GPT-3.5 ranked names linked to Black Americans top least often across 1,000 trials, failing the four-fifths (80%) hiring-discrimination rule.

title: Allocative discrimination - denial of jobs, credit, or services to protected groups
affected: job/credit/service applicants in protected demographic groups

name: Pre-deployment and ongoing demographic bias audit (disparate-impact / four-fifths testing, intersectional slices)
Protected-attribute data governance + counterfactual fairness constraints in model training

hazard: Models trained on historically biased data encode demographic correlations
hazardous_situation: An automated hiring/credit system scores applicants and is deployed without disparate-impact testing

title: LLMs degenerate into toxic content even from benign prompts
summary: RealToxicityPrompts (100k prompts) showed pretrained LMs emit toxic continuations even from non-toxic prompts with no failsafe detox method; ToxiGen (274k statements) demonstrated large-scale implicit hate generation across 13 minority groups.

title: Companion chatbots can expose vulnerable users to psychologically harmful content
summary: The Garcia v. Character Technologies case (AIID 826) documents a 14-year-old's suicide after prolonged engagement with a Character.AI chatbot that failed to intervene on suicidal ideation; Google/Character.AI settled related cases in Jan 2026, a landmark AI-harm settlement.

title: Psychological harm from exposure to hateful, harassing, or self-harm-promoting AI content
